lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This is fifty dollars.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Four years in a kitchen drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So who's had it all this time?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Not Maya. Not her grandma.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Birthday card. Little heart on the envelope.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: I was saving it for something special.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Shh. Follow the money.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Maya's not careless. She's normal.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: More than four in ten American adults have a gift card they haven't used.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The average? $244 each.
lines.spoken: The average? Two hundred and forty-four dollars each.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Add it up and it's about $27 billion.
lines.spoken: Add it up and it's about twenty-seven billion dollars.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In drawers, wallets, old phone apps.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Doing a job. Just not for us.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Then for who?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: When Maya's grandma bought that card, the store got fifty dollars. Cash. That day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But the store didn't sell anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No sweater left the shelf. No book. Nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So accountants don't call it a sale. They call it a liability.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The store owes whoever holds the card fifty dollars of stuff.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It's an IOU. And IOUs have a funny feature.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Until you show up, the money just sits with the store.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No interest. No rent. No questions.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Free money. Until you come back.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now picture that at the size of a coffee chain.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Starbucks customers load money onto cards and the app before they order.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Auto-reload, ten here, twenty-five there.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: At the end of 2023, Starbucks owed about $2.2 billion on cards and rewards.
lines.spoken: At the end of twenty twenty-three, Starbucks owed about two point two billion dollars on cards and rewards.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Money that's paid, but not yet spent.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: If you lent a bank two billion dollars, it would pay you interest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Lend it to a coffee shop and you get… coffee. Later. Maybe.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That's why people joke that Starbucks is a bank that sells coffee.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It isn't a bank. But for that money, it gets the best part of being one.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Cheap money. Very cheap.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But that's not the strange part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The strange part is the money nobody ever comes back for.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every year, some balances never get spent.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: $3.17 left on a card. A card lost in a move.
lines.spoken: Three dollars and seventeen cents left on a card. A card lost in a move.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Retailers have a word for that money: breakage.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They look at years of history and estimate how much you'll never use.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then they count it as revenue.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In one year, Starbucks booked about $188 million of it.
lines.spoken: In one year, Starbucks booked about a hundred and eighty-eight million dollars of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That's coffee nobody drank.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Coffee. Nobody. Drank.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And why do we forget? Because a gift card doesn't feel like money.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It feels like a gift. And gifts get saved.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: For something special.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Something special is how it ends up in a drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So here's the catch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A gift card is two gifts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One to the person you give it to.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And one to the store. A free loan.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And if life gets busy, it never has to be paid back.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Case closed?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Not yet. Because this time, the rules are on Maya's side.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Under US federal rules, most store gift cards can't expire within 5 years.
lines.spoken: Under US federal rules, most store gift cards can't expire within five years.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Five years from when the money was loaded. Maya's four-year-old card? Still good.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And no inactivity fees until a card's gone a full year unused.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Some states go further.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In California, under $15 left? You can ask for cash.
lines.spoken: In California, under fifteen dollars left? You can ask for cash.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So, tonight. Three things.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Open the drawer. Photograph every card and write down the balance.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Spend the smallest ones first. Those are the ones you'll lose.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And if you're giving one, give it for a place they already go. Every week.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Maya did one more thing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Her grandma always told her to read one book. She never had.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fifty dollars. Four years late.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It still counts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every gift card has a clock on it. And it's not the expiry date.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It's you, forgetting.

lines.speaker: nickel
lines.text: Check your drawer.
